title: The Task 2 Essay Playbook
subtitle: A step-by-step method for planning, writing and checking a clear IELTS Academic essay
description: This book gives you a simple, repeatable method for the IELTS Academic Writing Task 2 essay. You will learn to read the question, take a clear position, plan quickly, write developed paragraphs and check your work.
audience: Learners at Band 6-7 who want a clear method for Task 2 essays in a 40-minute practice.

chapters.title: Task 2 at a Glance: What You Are Writing and How It Is Marked
chapters.summary: A quick orientation to the Task 2 essay, the four marking criteria and the shape of a Band 6-7 answer.
chapters.body:
Task 2 is the second part of the Academic Writing test. You write an essay of at least 250 words in response to a point of view, an argument or a problem. The whole Writing test lasts 60 minutes. A sensible plan is to spend about 20 minutes on Task 1 and about 40 minutes on Task 2. Task 2 counts double, so it has more influence on your Writing band than Task 1.

This book gives you one repeatable method. You will learn to read the question, choose a position, plan, write each part of the essay and check it. Follow the method in every practice essay until it feels natural.

## How your essay is marked

Examiners use four criteria, and each one is worth the same share of your score:

- Task Response: you answer every part of the question and keep a clear position from start to finish.
- Coherence and Cohesion: your ideas are in a logical order, your paragraphs are clear and your linking is natural.
- Lexical Resource: you use a range of accurate and suitable vocabulary.
- Grammatical Range and Accuracy: you use a mix of simple and complex sentences, and most of them are correct.

There is no separate "ideas mark" or "grammar mark". A good plan helps Task Response and Coherence. Clear paragraphs help Coherence. Careful editing helps Grammar and Vocabulary. Every skill in this book supports at least one criterion.

## What a Band 6-7 essay looks like

At Band 6, an essay usually answers the question and has a visible structure, but some ideas are thin or unclear. At Band 7, the position is clear in the whole essay, and the main ideas are explained and supported. You do not need rare words or very long sentences. You need a clear answer and ideas that are developed properly.

## The shape we will use

Most strong Task 2 essays have four paragraphs:

- Introduction: two or three sentences that answer the question.
- Body paragraph 1: one main idea, explained and supported.
- Body paragraph 2: a second main idea, explained and supported.
- Conclusion: two sentences that repeat your position.

Some questions suit a different shape, and Chapter 2 shows you when. The skeleton stays the same.

Example: Imagine the question asks whether students should learn practical skills at school, such as cooking or first aid. A Band 6-7 answer might say yes, give one paragraph on daily life and one on emergencies, and then close with the same opinion. It is simple, but every part is connected.

## Common early mistakes

- Starting to write before understanding the question.
- Writing a general essay on the topic instead of answering the exact question.
- Writing only 230 or 240 words because time ran out.
- Giving many ideas with no explanation.

Tip: Treat the 250-word minimum as a floor, not a target. Most learners at this level write about 270 to 300 words in a four-paragraph essay. Aim for that range, and do not push the length much beyond it. A longer essay gives you more chances to make errors and uses time you need for checking.

In the next chapters, we build the essay one piece at a time. Keep a notebook or a folder of your practice essays, because you will use them for the revision plan in Chapter 7.
takeaways: Task 2 is at least 250 words and counts double in your Writing band.
Four equally weighted criteria are marked: Task Response, Coherence and Cohesion, Lexical Resource, and Grammatical Range and Accuracy.
A clear position and developed ideas matter more than rare words.
A four-paragraph essay is a reliable shape for most questions.
chapters.exercise: Write the four criteria from memory with one sentence on what each one rewards. Then check your list against this chapter.

chapters.title: Reading the Question and Spotting the Essay Type
chapters.summary: Learn to break a Task 2 question into parts and match it to the right essay structure.
chapters.body:
Many learners lose marks before they write a single sentence. They read the topic and start writing about it. Examiners mark how well you answer the question, not how much you know about the topic. So the first minute of Task 2 is for careful reading.

## Find three things in the question

Read the question twice. The first time, find the topic. The second time, find the task words and any limits.

- Topic: what is the general subject? For example, public transport, online shopping or working from home.
- Task words: what are you being asked to do? For example, discuss, agree or disagree, explain causes, suggest solutions.
- Limits: which words narrow the question? Look for words such as young people, in cities, in your country, or in the future.

Underline all three. If you ignore a limit, your answer may drift away from the question.

## The five common essay types

Most questions fit one of these types:

- Opinion (agree or disagree): "To what extent do you agree or disagree?" You give your view and support it.
- Discussion: "Discuss both views and give your opinion." You explain each side and then give your own view.
- Advantages and disadvantages: You explain both and often say which is stronger.
- Problem and solution (or cause and solution): You explain the problems or causes, then suggest realistic answers.
- Two-part question: Two direct questions, such as "Why is this happening? Is it a positive or negative development?" You answer both.

Some questions mix types. Read the final instruction carefully, because that tells you what to do.

Example: "Some people think that city governments should spend money on public parks. Others believe the money should be used for roads. Discuss both views and give your opinion." The topic is government spending. The task words are discuss both views and give your opinion. This is a discussion essay, so you need three things: park view, road view and your own view.

## Match the type to a structure

- Opinion: introduction with your position, two reasons in two body paragraphs, conclusion.
- Discussion: introduction, one paragraph for each view, with your opinion clear in the introduction and conclusion.
- Advantages and disadvantages: one paragraph for each side, or a comparison if the question asks "do the advantages outweigh the disadvantages?"
- Problem and solution: one paragraph for problems, one for solutions.
- Two-part question: one body paragraph for each question.

## Check every part

Before you move on, write a short checklist in the margin. For the parks question it might say: view A, view B, my opinion. After you finish writing, you will use this checklist again to confirm that nothing is missing.

Tip: Do not change the question words too much when you write. You must paraphrase in your introduction, but keep the meaning exact. If the question says "young people", do not write "all people".

Tip: If you are unsure about the type, look at the last sentence of the question. It is almost always the real instruction.
takeaways: Read the question twice and underline the topic, the task words and the limits.
Learn the five common types and the structure each one needs.
The last sentence of the question usually contains the real instruction.
Write a short checklist of required parts and use it again at the end.
chapters.exercise: Take any Task 2 question from your practice material. Name its type, underline the topic, task words and limits, and list the parts your essay must contain.

chapters.title: Forming a Clear Position
chapters.summary: Decide what you think, keep it consistent, and avoid the unclear answers that cost Task Response marks.
chapters.body:
A clear position is one of the most important parts of Task Response. The examiner should be able to say, in one sentence, what your answer is. If the examiner cannot, your Task Response score may suffer.

## What a position is

A position is your direct answer to the question. It is not a description of the topic. Compare these two sentences about working from home:

- "Working from home is a popular topic today." This describes the topic. It is not a position.
- "Working from home brings more benefits than drawbacks for most employees." This is a position.

The second sentence tells the reader what you will argue. Everything in your essay should then support it.

## How to choose quickly

You do not need to hold the most original opinion. You need the opinion that you can support best in about 270 words. Use this method:

- Write one quick reason for each side in two minutes at most.
- Choose the side where your reasons are clearer and your examples are easier.
- Do not choose a side only because it sounds clever. If you cannot explain it in simple English, it is a poor choice for the exam.

Example: The question asks whether children should have mobile phones before the age of twelve. You think both sides have points. Your reasons for "no" are easy: distraction during study, less time for family and less sleep. Your reasons for "yes" are weaker. Choose "no", and keep it clear.

## Partly agree is allowed, but be careful

For an opinion question, you can partly agree. This can be a good answer if you state it clearly. For example: "I agree that technology helps children learn, but only when parents set clear limits." The problem is that many learners say "partly" and then never explain which part. If you take a balanced position, your body paragraphs must match it exactly: one for what you accept, one for what you do not.

## Keep the position all the way through

A frequent error is to say "I agree" in the introduction and then argue the opposite in the second body paragraph. The examiner sees a changing answer. To prevent this:

- Write your position in the plan using one short sentence.
- Check each body paragraph against that sentence.
- Make sure the conclusion repeats the same view.

## Discussion and other types

In a discussion essay, you may be asked to give your own opinion, and then you must do so clearly. If the question does not ask for your opinion, you can still make a short clear statement, but your main job is to cover the task fairly. In an advantages and disadvantages question, state which side you find stronger if the question asks.

## Use language that sounds sure

Useful phrases include "I firmly believe that", "In my view", "I would argue that" and "This essay will argue that". Avoid weak phrases such as "maybe", "I am not sure" and "it depends" in your main position.

Tip: Do not use "I think" in every paragraph. Use it once or twice, then state your ideas directly.

Your position gives the essay direction. The next chapter shows how to turn it into a plan in five minutes.
takeaways: A position is a direct answer to the question, not a description of the topic.
Choose the side you can explain best, not the side that sounds most impressive.
If you partly agree, say exactly which part and make the paragraphs match.
Keep the same view in the introduction, the body and the conclusion.
chapters.exercise: For the question 'Should schools in Bangladesh teach financial skills?', write a one-sentence position and two quick reasons. Then check that both reasons support the same view.

chapters.title: Planning in Five Minutes
chapters.summary: A simple planning routine that gives you clear ideas and a safe structure before you write.
chapters.body:
Some learners skip planning because they fear running out of time. In practice, a short plan saves time. It stops you from stopping in the middle of a paragraph, searching for an idea. It also helps Coherence and Cohesion, because your ideas are already in order.

Aim for five minutes of planning. Here is one way to use them.

## Minute 1: Understand the question

Underline the topic, the task words and the limits, as you practised in Chapter 2. Write the essay type next to the question. Write your position in one short sentence.

## Minutes 2 to 3: Collect ideas

Think of two main ideas for your body paragraphs. For each one, find a reason and an example. Use a simple grid like this on your question paper:

- Main idea
- Why? (explanation)
- Example (specific and realistic)

Do not write full sentences. Use two or three words for each point.

Example: Question: Should public transport be free in big cities? Position: Yes, with limits.
Idea 1: Traffic. Why: fewer private cars. Example: Dhaka roads at peak hours.
Idea 2: Fairness. Why: low-income workers spend a large part of income on fares. Example: garment workers travelling daily.

Good examples do not have to be famous facts. They can be general, realistic situations. You should not invent numbers or statistics. Write "many workers" or "a large number of commuters", not "73 percent of commuters".

## Minute 4: Check the plan

Ask yourself three questions:

- Does each idea directly support my position?
- Are my two ideas different from each other?
- Have I covered every part of the question?

If two ideas are too similar, replace one. If an idea needs a long explanation with advanced vocabulary, choose a simpler idea.

## Minute 5: Order the paragraphs

Put your stronger idea first in most cases. In a discussion essay, put the view you disagree with first and your own view second, so your final body paragraph is close to your conclusion. Write 1 and 2 beside the ideas.

## Plan for the right size

You have room for two developed body paragraphs, not four. Many learners plan five ideas and then cannot develop any of them. Two ideas with explanation will usually score better than five ideas with no depth.

## When no ideas come

This happens to everyone. Use a thinking tool:

- Think of effects on individuals, families, society and the economy.
- Think of short-term and long-term results.
- Think about your own city or a relative's situation.

Pick the two most useful ideas, not the first two that appear.

Tip: Practise planning without writing the whole essay. Take five questions and write only the plans in 25 minutes. You will improve quickly, and you will not feel tired from writing five full essays.

Tip: Do not copy memorised ideas from sample essays. Examiners can see when the ideas do not fit the question.
takeaways: A five-minute plan saves time and improves coherence.
Plan two main ideas, each with a reason and a realistic example.
Do not invent statistics. Use general, believable examples.
Check the plan against the question before you start writing.
chapters.exercise: Set a timer for five minutes and plan an essay on 'Should public transport be free in big cities?' using the grid in this chapter. Check that your two ideas are different.

chapters.title: Introductions and Conclusions That Do Their Job
chapters.summary: Write short, clear opening and closing paragraphs that answer the question and support your position.
chapters.body:
The introduction and the conclusion are short, but they matter. The introduction shows the examiner your answer immediately. The conclusion shows that your answer stayed the same. Together they support Task Response and Coherence.

## The two-part introduction

A strong introduction for Band 6-7 usually has two or three sentences:

- Sentence 1: Paraphrase the question. Say the same thing in your own words.
- Sentence 2: Give your position, and say what the essay will cover.

Do not write a long general opening about the history of the world or modern life. Examiners do not reward it, and it uses time.

Example: Question: Some people believe that it is better to live in a big city than in a village. To what extent do you agree?

Introduction: "Many people think that urban life is superior to life in the countryside. I partly agree with this view, because cities offer better job opportunities, although villages provide a healthier and calmer way of living."

Notice the parts. The first sentence paraphrases. The second states the position and gives a preview of both body paragraphs.

## How to paraphrase safely

- Change words with the same meaning: "believe" to "think", "better" to "superior".
- Change the structure: "It is better to live in a city" to "City life is preferable".
- Keep the key meaning exact. Do not change "young people" into "everyone".
- Do not paraphrase words that have no good substitute, such as "internet" or "government".

If you cannot paraphrase a word, keep it and change the words around it.

## Mistakes in introductions

- Copying the question word for word.
- Writing "In this essay I will talk about" and nothing else.
- Giving a long background paragraph.
- Missing the position.

## The short, strong conclusion

The conclusion usually has two sentences, and it should do only two things:

- Restate your position in new words.
- Summarise your main reasons in one clause.

Example: "In conclusion, although cities offer valuable career opportunities, I believe that village life is better for health and family relationships. Therefore, people should choose where to live according to what matters most to them."

Do not bring in new ideas in the conclusion. If you have a new thought, it belongs in a body paragraph or nowhere.

## Make the conclusion match the introduction

Read your introduction and your conclusion together. They should say the same thing. If the introduction says "I partly agree" and the conclusion says "I strongly disagree", the examiner will notice.

## Signal words

Useful opening words for a conclusion are "In conclusion", "To sum up" and "Overall". Use only one. Do not write "In conclusion" and "To sum up" together.

Tip: Write the introduction last if you often get stuck at the start. Plan the essay, write the body paragraphs, and then write the introduction when your ideas are clear. Many learners find this easier. Just leave space at the top of the page.
takeaways: An introduction has two parts: a paraphrase and a clear position.
Paraphrase by changing words and structure, but keep the meaning exact.
A conclusion restates your position and main reasons without new ideas.
The introduction and conclusion must agree with each other.
chapters.exercise: Write a two-sentence introduction and a two-sentence conclusion for this question: 'Some people think that university education should be free. Do you agree or disagree?' Check that both give the same position.

chapters.title: Body Paragraphs with PEEL Development
chapters.summary: Use the PEEL pattern to turn each main idea into a clear, well-developed paragraph.
chapters.body:
Body paragraphs are where most of your marks are earned. A common problem at Band 5 and 6 is that learners state an idea and then move on. At Band 7, the idea is explained and supported. PEEL is a simple pattern that helps you do this.

## What PEEL means

- Point: the main idea of the paragraph, in one clear sentence.
- Explain: say what you mean and why it is true.
- Example: give a specific, realistic situation.
- Link: connect the idea back to the question or to your position.

A paragraph of five or six sentences with this pattern is usually enough. Aim for about 90 to 120 words in each body paragraph.

## Building a paragraph step by step

Example: Question: Do you agree that governments should spend more on public libraries?

Point: "Public libraries give students from poorer families access to learning resources."
Explain: "Many families cannot afford to buy textbooks or pay for a quiet study space, so a library can reduce the gap between rich and poor learners."
Example: "For instance, a student in a crowded home in Dhaka, with load-shedding in the evening, can study in a lit library instead of giving up homework."
Link: "As a result, library funding supports equal opportunity, which is a strong reason why governments should invest more."

Read the four parts. Each one has a different job. The example is realistic and does not use an invented statistic.

## Useful ways to explain

If you are stuck in the Explain step, ask yourself one of these questions:

- Why does this happen?
- What is the result of this?
- Who is affected?
- What would happen without it?

Answering one question in one or two sentences is enough.

## Good examples

An example does not have to be a famous event. It can be:

- A typical situation, such as a worker travelling in a crowded bus.
- A general comparison between two groups of people.
- Something from daily life during a festival, exam season or a power cut.

Avoid long personal stories. Avoid exact percentages and figures unless you are certain they are true. Words such as "many", "some" and "a large number of" are safer.

## Cohesion inside the paragraph

Use linking words, but do not overuse them. A simple set is enough:

- Adding: in addition, moreover, also.
- Contrast: however, although, whereas.
- Result: therefore, as a result, consequently.
- Example: for instance, for example, such as.

Tip: One linking word per sentence is too many. Use a link only when the relationship between ideas needs it. Refer back with words such as "this", "these students" and "such a situation" for smoother flow.

## Check your paragraph

After each paragraph, ask three questions. Does it have one main idea? Is the idea explained, not only stated? Does it support my position? If the answer is no, add or cut a sentence.

Use the same pattern for the second body paragraph. If the paragraphs have the same structure, your essay will feel organised and balanced.
takeaways: PEEL stands for Point, Explain, Example, Link.
Each body paragraph needs one main idea, developed in five or six sentences.
Use realistic examples and avoid invented statistics.
Use linking words only where the relationship between ideas needs them.
chapters.exercise: Write one PEEL paragraph of about 100 words on why public libraries are useful. Label the four parts in the margin.

chapters.title: Editing, Timing and Your Revision Plan
chapters.summary: Use a final checking routine, a clear timetable for the 40 minutes, and a four-week plan to keep improving.
chapters.body:
Writing the essay is only part of the job. A short, careful check can raise your accuracy and protect your Lexical Resource and Grammar marks. This chapter gives you a timetable for the exam and a revision plan for the weeks before it.

## A 40-minute timetable

Use this as a guide for Task 2:

- 5 minutes: read the question and plan.
- 27 to 28 minutes: write the essay.
- 5 minutes: check and correct.

Practise this timing at home. If you finish writing early, spend the extra time checking. If you run out of time, do not rush a long conclusion. Write two short sentences and stop.

## Your checking routine

Read your essay once from the beginning, slowly, with a pen. Check one area at a time:

- Task: Did I answer every part? Is my position clear from the introduction to the conclusion?
- Words: Is the essay at least 250 words? Count your lines to estimate.
- Grammar: Check subject-verb agreement, articles, plurals and tenses. Many learners at this level repeat the same small mistakes.
- Spelling and punctuation: Check capital letters, full stops and commas.
- Vocabulary: Replace repeated words, but only if you know a correct replacement.

Tip: Keep a personal error list. If you often forget "the", or write "peoples", or mix up "its" and "it's", write these on a small card. Check for those exact errors first.

## Handwriting and neatness

If you write on paper, make sure the examiner can read every word. If you take the test on a computer, check the screen for typing mistakes before you submit. If you change a word, cross it out neatly and write the correct word clearly.

## Common timing problems and fixes

- Spending ten minutes on the introduction: write two sentences, then move on.
- Planning for fifteen minutes: set a timer and stop at five.
- Having no time for the conclusion: practise writing it in under two minutes.
- Writing too many words: stay close to 270 to 300 words.

## A four-week revision plan

Week 1: Question analysis. Take ten questions and identify the type, the task words and the limits. Do not write essays yet.

Week 2: Planning and paragraphs. Write five plans each day for three days. Then write three PEEL paragraphs each week.

Week 3: Full essays. Write two timed essays this week, one opinion and one discussion. Use the checklist from Chapter 2 and the checking routine above.

Week 4: Mixed practice. Write one essay of each of the remaining types: advantages and disadvantages, problem and solution, and two-part question. Compare your first and last essays and note what has improved.

After each essay, write down two things you did well and two things to fix. Read your error list before every new essay.

## Keep going

Progress in Writing is gradual. Your goal is not a perfect essay on the first try. It is a clear method that you can repeat under exam conditions. If possible, ask a teacher or a trusted study partner to read your essays, and compare their comments with the four marking criteria.
takeaways: Use a timetable: about 5 minutes planning, 27 to 28 writing, 5 checking.
Check task, word count, grammar, spelling and vocabulary in that order.
Keep a personal error list and read it before every essay.
Follow the four-week plan and review your progress after each essay.
chapters.exercise: Write your own timetable for a 40-minute Task 2 practice and list your three most common errors. Use them as your checking card for the next essay.
